item.title: Comparative O-Glycosylation Analysis of Etanercept Originator and Biosimilars Using Orthogonal LC-MS Workflows
item.description: Etanercept is a highly glycosylated Fc-fusion protein whose dense, heterogeneous O-glycosylation is challenging to characterize yet relevant to biosimilarity assessment. We compared O-glycosylation in five originator (Enbrel) batches, three biosimilars (Erelzi, Benepali and Nepexto) and the EDQM chemical reference standard using orthogonal LCMS workflows on an Orbitrap Excedion Pro BioPharma mass spectrometer. Native intact mass analysis after N-glycan and sialic acid removal, and middle-up analysis after IdeS digestion, characterized O-glycan macroheterogeneity together with C-terminal lysine and N-terminal leucine-loss variants. Site-specific mapping combined the O-glycoproteases OgpA and IMPa with HCD-triggered EThcD fragmentation. The same 13 O-glycosites were identified in every sample, carrying predominantly sialylated core 1 O-glycans (72%-80% sialylated) with low levels of Tn antigen. In contrast, Benepali and Nepexto showed lower O-glycan occupancy (approximately 17.3 versus 18.9-19.1 O-glycans per molecule) and broader glycoform distributions, and Benepali showed markedly elevated leucine loss (35% of TNF domains). Subunit analysis resolved nearisobaric leucine-loss and di-lysine variants that were ambiguous at the intact level, while EThcD localized O-glycans within densely glycosylated peptides. This multi-level workflow provides a generalizable approach for site-specific O-glycosylation analysis and comparability assessment of O-glycosylated biotherapeutics.

item.title: Polarization Is Required to Model Electrostatic Preorganization: The Case of Chorismate Mutase
item.description: Electrostatic preorganization contributes to enzymatic catalysis through transition state stabilization and is often investigated using classical molecular dynamics (MD) simulations that employ fixed-charge force fields (FFs). Although polarizable FFs allow for more accurate quantification of local electrostatic effects, whether they qualitatively differ from fixed-charge FFs regarding properties such as the substrate conformation stabilized by the enzyme's electrostatics remains unclear. Here, we compare molecular dynamics simulations of chorismate mutase performed with the AMOEBA polarizable FF and the AMBER fixed-charge FF. We find that simulations using AMOEBA sample chorismate geometries resembling the transition state-like near attack conformation (NAC), while AMBER simulations sample strictly non-NAC conformations. The local substrate-protein interactions are also completely altered by the choice of FF, with AMOEBA and AMBER each sampling distinct active site hydrogen bond networks. Finally, even at matched reactive substrate conformations, the heterogeneous three-dimensional electric field experienced by the substrate is qualitatively different between the FFs. By additionally comparing to a modified AMOEBA FF with the induced dipole term turned off, we also isolate the explicit polarization in AMOEBA as the key contributor to these differences.

item.title: Large Language Models in Chemistry: Opportunities, Limitations, and Hallucination Risks
item.description: Large language models (LLMs) have moved quickly from general-purpose text tools to components of chemical research workflows. They are now used to extract data from the literature, propose synthesis routes, write analysis code, predict properties from few examples, and control laboratory instruments through tool-augmented agents. These capabilities create real opportunities, particularly for researchers and institutions with limited access to specialist software and training. They also carry risks that are specific to chemistry. Chemical information is dense with symbols, units, stoichiometry, and safety-critical numbers, and LLMs generate fluent text whether or not it is correct. This perspective reviews the main opportunities for LLMs in chemistry, the technical limitations that constrain them, and a taxonomy of hallucination types with examples of how each can cause harm in a laboratory or research setting. It then proposes a practical verification framework for everyday users, a set of reporting practices for authors, and a short research agenda. The central argument is that LLMs are most valuable in chemistry when they are treated as fallible assistants wrapped in verification tools, such as cheminformatics libraries, databases, and physical measurement, and not as sources of chemical truth.

item.title: Sequence order controls silver(I) coordination in aqueous His–Met–Pro tripeptide–nitrate mixtures: an ab initio molecular dynamics study
item.description: Silver–peptide interactions underpin peptide-directed synthesis of silver nanomaterials and the silver-resistance machinery of bacteria, yet the molecular-level speciation of Ag(I) in the presence of short peptides and nitrate remains poorly resolved. Here we report 100-ps ab initio molecular dynamics simulations of three sequence isomers of the tripeptide His–Met–Pro (HMP, HPM and PHM; 220 atoms each) in water, with four Ag(I) ions, four nitrate anions and 32 water molecules at 298 K, using the PBE–PAW description (VASP 6.1.0, 500 eV plane-wave cutoff, Γ-point sampling). In all three systems silver remains mononuclear, with average coordination numbers of 2.6–2.9 and only transient Ag–Ag contacts (present in 2–9% of frames at a 3.2 Å cutoff). The composition of the coordination shell is strongly sequence-dependent: His–Met–Pro is dominated by the His imidazole nitrogen (0.48 contacts per Ag) and nitrate oxygen (0.57), whereas His–Pro–Met is dominated by the Met thioether sulfur (0.73) with nitrate largely excluded (0.16); Pro–His–Met shows an intermediate, mixed N/S/nitrate shell and the largest peptide conformational rearrangement (heavy-atom RMSD 6.1 Å, radius of gyration 5.8 Å). Nitrate and water exchange on ∼0.2–1 ps timescales, while peptide N/S donors remain bound for several to tens of picoseconds. These results demonstrate that, at fixed composition, sequence order controls which donors are presented to Ag(I) and therefore the speciation from which silver nanomaterials nucleate.

item.title: Monomer sequence influences electron transport in aromatic amide foldamers
item.description: Sequence encodes structure and function in biomolecules, but whether monomer order influences electron transport in synthetic foldamers remains incompletely understood. Here, we investigate aromatic amide foldamers built from a peptide-inspired secondary amide and its N-methylated peptoid-inspired analogue. Single molecule conductance measurements reveal that the all-secondary-amide foldamer exhibits a well-defined conductance state (~10-3.8 G0), comparable to the substantially shorter secondary-amide building block (~10-3.7 G0), whereas incorporation of N-methylated units produces lower or less-defined conductance features. Notably, foldamers with identical composition but different sequence arrangements exhibit distinct conductance distributions, demonstrating that sequence order influences electron transport. Displacement and flicker noise analyses indicate compact junction geometries with substantial throughspace contributions, and the all secondary amide foldamer responds most strongly to changes in applied bias and molecular concentration. Computational modeling using molecular dynamics (MD) simulations, density functional theory (DFT), and nonequilibrium Green's function (NEGF)-DFT calculations provide insight into sequencedependent conformational variability. Overall, this work demonstrates that oligomerization can generate electron transport behavior that cannot be inferred directly from isolated monomer properties and establishes monomer order as a design variable for molecular electronics.

item.title: Probabilistic Design and Safety-Constrained Optimization of a Firewater-Powered Portable Valve Actuation System
item.description: Almost every hazardous facility owns a pressurized, regularly inspected source of hydraulic power: its firewater system. This study asks whether a portable water-hydraulic operator driven through a fire hose can stroke seized or stiff valves without overloading the stem or taking the water that firefighting needs, and which design and operating rules make that likely. A Monte Carlo model with an explicit hydraulic circuit, motor leakage, a relief valve and the surge on stall is evaluated on 200,000 draws; every added mechanism can be switched off, recovering the earlier first-order model exactly. Under assumed input distributions a baseline tool (200 cc, 250:1, 60 gpm) completes the stroke in 75% of the draws but without exceeding the allowable stem torque in only 63%, because a median surge of 45 psi accompanies the stall; a stroke needs about 1,600 L of water. A hose-side accumulator and a relief chart set from the stem strength reduce the over-torque probability to 1% (motor speed at most 3,000 rpm) at a cost of 3 to 9 percentage points of safe strokes, of which a slow creep flow at the start and end of travel recovers 4 to 6. The surge model reproduces classical water-hammer results. The optimum holds out of sample but not under a stem 30% weaker than its data sheet (14% over-torque), and the 2 firefighting reserve is protected only if the spare flow of the source is known. The results are simulation outputs under assumed priors, not measurements.

item.title: Measuring chemical safety and refusal in language models
item.description: A language model can decline a chemistry question for several reasons. It may detect a safety concern, fail to identify the molecule, or lack the facts needed to answer. When it does answer, the response may still be wrong or incomplete. Chemical safety evaluations need to distinguish these outcomes before interpreting differences between models. We propose a framework for doing so, using established practices from cheminformatics: verified identities and reference answers, suitable controls and baselines, independent validation, and statistics that account for related molecules and repeated measurements. We examine chemical safety studies, including SynthRefusal within onepot-Bench 0, ChemSafetyBench, DualChem, and broader scientific safety benchmarks. Eight detailed audits and additional methods readings identify both effective controls and gaps in the evidence. Our reanalyses reproduce large effects of molecular identifiers in ChemIDBench and system prompts in XSTest. A calculation from DualChem shows how excluding tool failures changes the apparent benefit of web access. Because these studies measure different outcomes, we do not pool their results. We propose an experiment that holds legitimate chemical safety questions fixed while changing the identifier and the information supplied to the model. It measures refusal and answer quality together, with separate judgments of whether withholding is appropriate. Separate extensions would test unsafe compliance and, where relevant, practical execution. Each proposed control addresses a specific uncertainty in interpreting model behavior.

item.title: Beyond Ion Features: Resolving Ion Redundancy for LC–HRMS/MS
item.description: Untargeted LC–HRMS/MS workflows frequently represent the same molecular entity through multiple ion features, including adducts, multimers, dehydrated species, and signals compatible with in-source fragmentation. This ion redundancy can propagate into downstream analyses, increasing apparent molecular-network complexity and contributing to unannotated features. To address this issue, we developed two workflows integrated into Compound Discoverer. The unresolved workflow enables structured export of MS2 spectra in MGF format with matched quantitative data, metadata, and an audit trail, whereas the resolved workflow performs ionredundancy resolution and representative-feature selection before export. The approach was evaluated using two reference-standard panels, comprising phytocannabinoids and novel psychoactive substances (NPS), and applied to plant, biological, and in vitro drug-metabolism datasets. Ion-redundancy patterns varied across chemical classes and analytical contexts, encompassing alternative ion species, predefined mass-difference relationships, and MS2-child matches, identified when the m/z of a lower-mass coeluting feature matched a product ion in the MS2 spectrum of a higher-mass feature. Across applications, the resolved workflow reduced exported MGF entries by 18.2–36.1%. In molecular networking, the workflow reshaped molecular-family composition and connectivity through spectral-quality filtering, feature removal, and representative-ion reassignment, while preserving chromatographically distinct features lacking sufficient evidence of redundancy. These findings suggest that LC–HRMS/MS feature space does not necessarily reflect the underlying molecular space. By addressing ion redundancy before spectral export, these workflows provide a conservative and traceable framework that reduces analytical complexity, addresses a potential contributor to the apparent dark metabolome, and enables a more interpretable spectral representation that may better reflect underlying molecular diversity.

item.title: Extended Inter-laboratory Characterization of the New Coastal Seawater Dissolved Organic Matter Reference Material TRM-0522
item.description: Dissolved organic matter (DOM) reference materials are critical to ensuring reliable comparability of measurements across experiments and between labs. TRM-0522, isolated in 2022 from 45 m deep seawater off of Sweden’s west coast, fills the niche of a previously unavailable coastal marine DOM reference material. After its isolation, we detailed a limited number of metrics for TRM-0522, initially disclosing Orbitrap high-resolution mass spectrometry, nuclear magnetic resonance, carbon proportion, absorbance, and fluorescence data. With TRM-0522 becoming more widely used, a variety of labs have generated different metrics that help to characterize and define the chemical properties of this coastal reference material. Here, we disclose TRM-0522 data from elemental analysis, isotopic analysis (δ13C and Δ14C signatures), condensed aromatic “black” carbon characterization, ultra-HRMS (10-21 Tesla FT-ICR-MS and Orbitrap Fusion Lumos), CD3 labelling, and contribution of carbonyls in absorbance and fluorescence after NaBH4 reduction, pH titration, and nitroxide quenching. This greatly expanded dataset reinforces TRM-0522’s suitability as a coastal reference material, and provides metrics for future use between labs and for inevitable additional large-scale collections of material from this site.

item.title: Spatiotemporal Decoupling of Antimicrobial and Osteogenic Cues for Tissue Regeneration: Evidence, Design Windows, and a Validation Roadmap
item.description: Infected bone defects require two outcomes that can conflict at the same site: reduction of biofilm-associated bacterial burden, which usually needs high local antimicrobial exposure, and regeneration of vascularised bone, which needs viable progenitor cells and a resolving immune environment. Biomaterials that present antimicrobial and regenerative cues together are clinically established, but in some systems the exposure needed to act on biofilm may approach the tolerance of host cells. This targeted narrative review develops spatiotemporal decoupling, the separation of cues in time, location or activation condition, as a design hypothesis rather than a proven superior strategy. It (i) defines decoupling operationally and classifies published platforms accordingly; (ii) frames the therapeutic window as a measurable exposure problem, defines exposure metrics, and specifies what must be measured to compute them; (iii) maps four overlapping biological domains (bacterial burden, inflammation, vascular supply, bone formation) to cues, controls and readouts, with each design rule tagged by evidence status; (iv) examines the immuneosteogenic–vascular network as a hypothesis map; (v) positions bioactive glasses and glass-ceramics as a testable platform opportunity, separating what has been shown from what is inferred; and (vi) sets out validation gates and author-proposed reporting recommendations. Most evidence reviewed is mechanistic or preclinical, and matched comparisons against equal-payload co-delivery remain the decisive missing experiment.

item.title: Chemistry-Informed Transfer and Interaction-Resolved Learning Towards Data-Efficient Materials Exploration
item.description: Optimizing synthesis parameters for new thin-film materials is slow and often relies on intuition and trial and error. Gaussian process (GP) models suit low-data settings, but treat each material separately or need engineered descriptors to learn across materials. Multi-task GPs share information across materials but infer these relationships solely from sparse data, making them unreliable early on. We introduce a chemistry-informed multi-task GP that derives these relationships from a Tanimoto kernel on molecular fingerprints, enabling knowledge transfer without descriptor engineering. In closed-loop, uncertaintydriven exploration of a seven-dimensional synthesis space, comprising one categorical variable (three chiral 2D hybrid organic-inorganic perovskite compositions) and six continuous synthesis parameters, we tested 287 conditions (<0.1% of the discretized synthesis space). Knowledge transfer matched the accuracy of single-task GPs trained on the full target dataset using between 35-60% of the target data. Interaction analysis revealed a three-way coupling among annealing temperature, precursor concentration, and composition. This coupling makes a one-variable-at-a-time optimization challenging. Our framework offers a simple strategy for transferring and interpreting knowledge across related materials.

item.title: Advanced High-Throughput Characterization of Nanoporous Materials using Pore Graphs
item.description: Nanoporous materials databases now contain millions of structures, yet the tools for characterizing their void spaces have not kept pace. Standard descriptors such as largest cavity diameter and pore limiting diameter are global quantities that conflate local pore geometry with inter-pore connectivity, and can hide distinct pores and network topology behind a single number. We present Mofography, an open-source Python/Rust library that recasts pore characterization as a three-dimensional image-processing problem. It segments the void space into non-overlapping pore regions, connects them at shared windows, and constructs a pore graph that decouples local properties (size, shape, chemistry) from global topology (percolation, connectivity). Global textural properties are obtained as queries on this graph and agree with those from Zeo++ and Pore-Blazer across a diverse set of metal-organic frameworks (MOFs), while remaining traceable to individual pores and windows. The same representation supports pore-resolved pore size distributions, multi-modal pore-type clustering, window detection across periodic boundaries, and percolation and accessibility analysis. To demonstrate its utility for material discovery, we develop a workflow integrated with Mofography to screen favorable pores in MOFs for xylene isomer separations and validate selected candidates with grand canonical Monte Carlo simulations. The results reveal how accessibility and competing pore environments influence whether local preferences translate into material performance. By linking global textural properties to local pore environments and their connectivity, Mofography provides a unique platform for interpreting structure–property relationships and accelerating nanoporous materials discovery.

item.title: Signed Kekulé structures and Hückel gap-closure thresholds in phenylenes
item.description: Naphthalene and biphenylene have comparable Hückel HOMO–LUMO gaps, yet no positive bond couplings close the gap of naphthalene, whereas coordinated changes of 18.9% close that of biphenylene. We define the gap-closure threshold as the smallest maximum relative change of existing bond couplings needed to close the gap. At equal reference couplings, it depends only on the signed Kekulé polynomial: it is maximal when all Kekulé structures share one sign, is fixed by a polynomial equation when one structure has the minority sign, and is otherwise bounded. Phenylenes with the same sequence of linear and angular annelations share the threshold, even when their gaps differ. For linear [N ]phenylenes it approaches π2/[4(N + 1)2]; angular [3]phenylene closes only by breaking mirror symmetry. In a bond-length model, the threshold ranks closure energies better than the relaxed gap does, and the predicted closing distortion is nearly the steepest-descent direction of the B3LYP Kohn–Sham gap (cosine 0.989).

item.title: Predicting Active and Inactive Targets of Small Molecules from ChEMBL Data Using the Polypharmacology Browser PPB4
item.description: Drug-like molecules often interact with multiple biological targets, which must be identified during drug development. Various models spanning classical machine learning, deep learning and artificial intelligence, predict active targets of a query molecule based on its structural similarity to target annotated molecules from drug-target interaction databases such as ChEMBL. Herein we report on the Polypharmacology Browser PPB4, a deep neural network trained on ChEMBL35. In contrast to its predecessor PPB3 and related tools which only return lists of probably active targets, PPB4 also lists probably inactive targets, as well as targets that are probably both active and inactive if the query molecule is similar to both active and inactive compounds for that target. Two prospective case studies illustrate the use of PPB4, which returns every predicted target together with the list of nearest neighbor molecules marked as active on that target in the training data. PPB4 is freely available at https://ppb4.gdb.tools.

item.title: OpenASChem: A Data Analysis Software Suite for High-Throughput Affinity Selection Mass Spectrometry
item.description: Summary: Affinity selection mass spectrometry (AS-MS) enables ligand discovery from pooled compound libraries, but compound signal assignment and cross-run review remain labor-intensive as screens expand across multiple targets. Here, we present OpenASChem, an open-source platform with a graphical interface for compoundcentric analysis of high-throughput pull-down ASMS screens. OpenASChem integrates standardguided peak matching, cross-run quantification and enrichment analysis with interactive chromatographic review. We evaluated OpenASChem using mixed-standard and AS-MS screening datasets acquired in our laboratory. In the mixed-standard benchmark, OpenASChem recovered 248 expectedpositive compounds compared with 204 using an XCMS-based workflow, a 21.6% increase, with no calls from the two pools expected to remain below the enrichment threshold. In a four-pool ASMS screen against eight proteins, it reported 13 candidate associations, including all five previously reported hits and two additional chromatographically supported candidates, while reducing candidates not supported by manual review by 86.7%. An interactive summary integrates results across pools and targets, helping laboratories assess chromatographic evidence and prioritize compounds for follow-up validation.

item.title: Training of Neural Network Machine Learning Potentials for Activation Barrier Calculations in Predicting Growth Modes of Deposited Metals
item.description: Machine-learning interatomic potentials (MLIPs) are opening many new opportunities to extend the capabilities of computational materials science. MLIPs deliver increased throughput and simulations at time and length scales beyond first principles density functional theory (DFT), while maintaining near-DFT accuracy, thus allowing unravelling of chemical processes not accessible with DFT. In this work, we present an approach to training a neural network MLIP using DeepMD-kit software that delivers both accurate energies and forces, suitable for determining activation energies via nudged elastic band calculations. We use the deposition of metals on substrates, in particular Ru and Cu on TaN for semiconductor device interconnects, as the example system, for which activation barriers of metal atom migration at the metal-substrate interface and on the metal deposit are important in understanding the evolution of the film morphology during deposition. The structure of the metal-substrate interface directly affects the performance of devices, from catalysts and sensors, to interconnects and contacts in nanoelectronics. The activation barrier energies from our MLIP for all sizes of metal atom deposits reproduce the DFT activation energies to within an average error of 0.08 eV (6%) for Cu and 0.23 eV (19%) for Ru. The trends of the DFT barriers are preserved by the MLIP and the computing time is reduced from days using high performance computing to minutes on a personal laptop. This allows us to assess the activation energies for complex processes such as the transition of a 2-layer metal cluster to a 3-layer cluster-a key step in metal island growth. Morphology evolution occurs on multiple scales, from initial nucleation, to layer growth and cluster ripening. By demonstrating that MLIPs can be used to accurately and rapidly deliver activation energies for the relevant atomic scale processes, a multi-scale predictive atomistic model of metal deposition and growth chemistry becomes feasible.

item.title: Mechanosensitive ion transport in hexagonal boron nitride nanopores
item.description: In biological systems, mechanical strain can trigger strong changes in ion conductance and signaling, yet in synthetic nanopores, achieving similar mechanosensitive behavior has been a significant challenge. Here, we demonstrate that subtle mechanical strain can induce strong modulation of ionic current in small hexagonal boron nitride (h-BN) nanopores. Using hydrostatic pressure to apply small lateral strain to free-standing single-layer h-BN membranes featuring triangular sub-1-nm nanopores, we observed ion conductance modulation exceeding 1 30% under 0.5% strain. We attribute this response to the strain-dependent interplay of ionpore and ion-water interactions within the nanopore. The measured mechanosensitivity values also agreed strongly with those obtained from modeling of strain-tunable transport in ensembles of h-BN nanopores. These findings establish a framework for developing strain-responsive membranes for applications in molecular separations and sensing.

item.title: Optical Properties of Different Chemistries of Natural and Synthetic Melanin
item.description: Melanin, a ubiquitous black pigment, consists of at least five chemistries identified by the starting monomers involved in its polymerization. Natural melanin may also contain other components, such as lipids and proteins, that can affect its optical properties. Melanin is known for its high refractive index and broadband absorption. However, most optical-property observations are based on measurements of eumelanin-based chemistry. In this study, we used spectroscopic ellipsometry to measure the complex refractive index over a broad wavelength range (380–1700 nm) for the three main melanin chemistries: eumelanin, allomelanin, and pheomelanin. We compared the complex refractive indices of these materials with values obtained from UV absorption measurements, using an integrating sphere to minimize scattering effects. Our results show that melanin chemistry strongly influences optical properties. Pheomelanin from human red hair has the lowest absorption and refractive index, while poly(L-3,4-dihydroxyphenylalanine) (PDOPA; a polydopamine-based eumelanin chemistry) has the highest refractive index and absorption. We also observed variation in the optical properties of pheomelanin samples extracted from human red hair and rooster feathers. Thus, variations in melanin composition affect both the optical and thermal properties of melanin, highlighting the need to identify its precise chemistry in natural systems to understand melanin's impact on function and performance.

item.title: Plasmon-Enhanced Nanosensing: From Single Proteins to Therapeutic Nanoparticles
item.description: Plasmonic nanosensing, in which plasmon-enhanced near fields are used for single-molecule detection andsingle-particlebiosensing,hasmovedbeyondensemblerefractive-indexmeasurements.Itnow interrogatesindividualproteins,transientmolecularcomplexes,photoexcitedredoxpartnersand heterogeneous therapeutic nanoparticles. Its defining advantage is not a universal detection limit. It is the ability to concentrate optical energy into nanometric volumes and to transduce properties that ensemble averagesconceal.Localizedsurfaceplasmonresonance,surface-enhancedRamanandinfrared spectroscopy, plasmon-enhanced fluorescence, nanoaperture optical trapping and hybrid optical–electrical nanopores each provide different observables: binding-induced spectral shifts, vibrational fingerprints, residence-time distributions, conformational fluctuations and particle-specific electrical signatures. This review synthesizes the electromagnetic, thermal and transport physics that govern these observables. It thenevaluatesrepresentativeapplications,fromsingle-proteindynamicsandweakprotein–protein interactionstowavelength-dependentcytochromec–cytochromecoxidasekinetics,single-virus detection, adeno-associated virus genome loading, extracellular vesicles and lipid nanoparticles. Unlike earlierreviewsorganizedbydeviceorbyenhancementmechanism,thisreviewtreatsplasmonic nanosensing as an inverse problem and a metrology problem. Particular attention is given to three issues: separatingmolecularheterogeneityfromspatiallyheterogeneousenhancement;separatinggenuine photochemistryfromphotothermalandresonance-detuningartifacts;andcorrectingclass-dependent capture before event counts are reported as sample composition.Closed-form illustrations show how capture bias and device-to-device variation can produce convincing but incorrect results. A minimuminformationreportingchecklistandamaturitymapareproposedsothatplasmonicsingle-entity measurementscanprogressfrom informativeresearchprobestotransferable,orthogonallyvalidated analytical methods.

item.title: vibyverse: an integrated computational chemistry ecosystem developed through agentic engineering
item.description: We describe the vibyverse, developed by agentic engineering, comprising vibe-sketcher for chemical structures and reaction schemes, vibe-qc for electronic-structure calculations, vibe-scheduler for execution and retrieval, vibe-viewer for inspection and presentation, and the Quantum Visualization Format (QVF) for structured exchange. The workflow starts with reaction design in vibe-sketcher, submission through vibe-scheduler, calculation with vibe-qc, and inspection and analysis in vibe-viewer, with scientific data transferred through QVF. We examine the responsibilities of each component and the information that must survive their connections, including charge, multiplicity, geometry, method settings, runtime identity and result provenance. Source inspection identifies implemented interfaces and their compatibility requirements. A Diels–Alder preparation example connects an editable scheme and preoptimized structures to validated QVF and viewer exports. The executed numerical workflow proceeds through MACE geometry optimization, PBE/def2-SVP refinement and DLPNO-CCSD(T) endpoint energies. A proposed water-on-boronnitride example would extend the workflow to periodic structures. The molecular optimization and Hessian use existing PBE routes without an added dispersion correction. Both Hessian stencils identify minima for all three molecules. With an explicit restrictedreference contract, the correlated electronic energy of cyclohexene relative to butadiene and ethene is −190.547 kJ mol−1. Changing from TightPNO to NormalPNO shifts it by +0.187 kJ mol−1. The viewer reproduces both electronic reaction energies from the archived endpoints, in agreement with an independent stoichiometric sum. All data supporting this study are openly available from the Zenodo repository under accession number 23976098 at https://zenodo.org/records/23976098.

item.title: How do the research evaluation requirements of Chinese universities, which are oriented towards paper publication, affect the development of chemistry graduate students and faculty members?
item.description: Research assessment oriented towards publication has become an important feature of academic work, profoundly shaping the expectations for research productivity and the career advancement trajectories of researchers. However, its impact on graduate education in chemistry and the cultivation of independent researchers still requires further exploration. This qualitative study examines how publication requirements affect chemistry professors and graduate students in Chinese universities. Specifically, this research investigates how journal classification/ranking and publication goals intervene in the daily guidance practices of departments and mentors, how young teachers and graduate students respond to these expectations, and how assessment practices affect research autonomy, task allocation, researcher development, and career planning. Through thematic analysis of interview data, this study identified the institutional requirements, the mentoring practices of mentors, and their impact on the research training of graduate students. The research results revealed three interrelated processes: Firstly, the requirements of institutions for high-quality paper publication, access to research funds, and periodic performance evaluations were transformed into expectations within the research groups, in some cases even evolving into graduation requirements exceeding the official standards of the school; Secondly, teachers' coping strategies were to prioritize research projects with more predictable publication outcomes, while graduate students had to deal with the expectations of their mentors that might affect their research priorities and the completion of their degrees; Thirdly, these practices shaped the opportunities for students to explore independent research questions, participate in scientific decision-making, and plan their careers. The interviews also revealed contrasting results, including the improvement of research skills, supportive mentoring practices, and the loss of employment opportunities due to delayed graduation.

item.title: Goggles On, Bagels Out: A Randomized Hazard Hunt in a Browser Replica of a Real Teaching Laboratory
item.description: Students are usually introduced to the layout of a teaching laboratory, and to where its eyewash, shower, extinguisher and waste containers are, during a safety lecture on the first day of lab, a session that also covers the syllabus and the first experiment. I built a walkable, browser-based replica of the actual laboratory my students use, from a phone scan and photographs of the room, and turned it into a safety inspection. Each time a student opens the virtual lab, five hazards drawn at random from thirty-one are hidden in the room. Every hazard is tied to a rule in the course syllabus, from a drink on a bench or a fume hood sash left wide open to a classmate without goggles or a sleeve on fire. Students find and click each hazard, read what is wrong and what to do, carry out hands-on tasks such as dropping a used needle in the sharps container or guiding a splashed classmate to the eyewash, answer an emergency question, evacuate by the posted route when a fire alarm sounds, and finish with a report of what they found and missed. The inspection sits between a safety prelab page and the graded safety quiz in the learning management system; students must score at least 70% on the quiz before they are admitted to the lab room. The replica runs in an ordinary web browser with no headset or installation, downloads in about 31 MB, and was built by one instructor with a phone, free or low-cost software and generative AI tools. This report describes how the replica was built, how the hazards were designed and how the module fits into a course. Student outcomes will be evaluated in a later study.

item.title: Freestanding FeS2-Integrated Reduced Graphene Oxide Aerogels Enhance Cathode-to-Cell Electron Transfer in Three-Dimensional Living Cathodes
item.description: Three-dimensional (3D) living cathodes can retain dense biofilms, but cells within porous scaffolds may remain electronically underutilized. Here, we integrate FeS2 nanoparticles throughout a freestanding reduced graphene oxide (rGO) aerogel, combining interconnected macropores, continuous electron pathways, and spatially distributed FeS2 interfaces within a living cathode. This architecture provides three complementary functions: 3D biofilm retention, low-resistance cathode-to-cell electron delivery, and greater availability of intracellular reducing equivalents for fumarate reduction by Shewanella oneidensis MR-1. Compared to pristine rGO, FeS2-rGO generated a ~ 12-fold higher cathodic current density, accelerated complete fumarate depletion within 50 h, and reached 67% Faradaic efficiency to succinate. FeS2-rGO also exhibited a 2.4~4.1-fold higher biomass-normalized succinate partial current, the lowest fitted interfacial resistance, and the highest NADH/NAD+ ratio. Less than 2% of the loaded Fe dissolved, as measured by ICP-OES, while the characteristic FeS2-associated diffraction features were retained after operation. Mechanistically, mutant strain responses further showed that FeS2 strengthened electron transfer through the native outer membrane cytochrome-CymA network. By positioning electronically connected FeS2 interfaces throughout a freestanding porous electrode, this work combines long-range scaffold conduction with enhanced local, pathway-dependent electron uptake in a 3D living cathode.

item.title: Interaction without an interaction module
item.description: The prevailing way to model a many-body system is to encode every component and then let a module capture interaction. We show that the explicit interaction module is harmful when the number of components increases. We use a simple interaction-carrying encoder that compresses a component’s interaction contribution into its representation, and combine the representations by linear aggregation. This modelling approach is simple in form yet delivers unexpectedly excellent performance: it matches the prevailing explicit route under most conditions and exceeds it when a mixture carries more components than the training set covered. Moreover, an encoder produced this way has a clear advantage over per-component descriptors when it is transferred to a similar task: it greatly reduces the data requirements.

item.title: Protonation-state-dependent charge transfer to solvent in aqueous L-cysteine probed by resonant Auger–Meitner spectroscopy
item.description: Charge-transfer-to-solvent (CTTS) couples electronic, nuclear, and solvent dynamics on femtosecond timescales. In biologically relevant L-cysteine, resolving how protonation and local hydrogen bonding influence CTTS upon resonant excitation remains challenging. Sulfur KLL resonant Auger–Meitner spectroscopy qualitatively resolves different final states separated in kinetic energy. These include localized excited states, delocalized CTTS states, and the charge-transfer continuum, enabling direct identification of different decay channels in L-cysteine. At pH 12, the dianion exhibits a pronounced charge-transfer channel extending below the ionization threshold, negligible at pH 5. Transition-potential density functional theory and Born–Oppenheimer molecular dynamics link this to enhanced thiolate hydrogen-bond coordination, revealing a delocalized core-excited state nearly degenerate with the bright localized resonance. A Fano-based core-hole-clock approach, accounting for coherent population of the localized state and charge-transfer continuum, yields a charge-transfer time of 43± 8 fs, compared with 15± 2 fs from conventional core-hole-clock analysis, highlighting the importance of accounting for direct excitation into the chargetransfer continuum and its coherent coupling to the localized core-excited state when extracting charge-transfer times. Together, these results establish resonant Auger–Meitner spectroscopy with Fano-based analysis as a general strategy for probing protonation-and solvation-dependent ultrafast electronic delocalization in aqueous biomolecules.

item.title: High-resolution relaxometry suggests the presence of pervasive nano-second sugar motions in a DNA duplex.
item.description: Nucleic acids are central to many biomolecular processes central to cellular life, yet characterising their molecular motions and fluctuations with atomic resolution remains challenging. We introduce high-resolution relaxometry, combined with high-field nuclear spin relaxation, as a powerful tool to probe motions in nucleic acids. After recording an extensive spin-relaxation dataset from 2 to 23 T, we propose a framework, within the model-free approach, that allowed us to identify motions occurring both on the picosecond and low nanosecond time scales. By integrating these results with molecular dynamics simulations and ensembles, obtained from residual dipolar coupling (RDC) measurements, we propose a time-resolved model that includes fast helical motions and slower pervasive sugar puckering motions. The approach outlined in this study also provides a framework for interrogating molecular dynamics in nucleic acids with spin relaxation experiments and benchmarking molecular dynamics simulations that aim to characterise dynamic processes.

item.title: Toward Chemical Accuracy in Biomolecular Simulations through Data-Driven Many-Body Potentials: III. A Library of Amino Acid Building Blocks
item.description: Extending data-driven many-body potentials to peptides and proteins requires reusable building blocks that capture the chemical diversity of amino acids. Building on the many-body expansion (MBE) of the energy, we construct an intramolecular MB-nrg library for all 20 natural amino-acid residues by combining physics-based interactions with machine-learned (ML) n-body terms trained on DLPNO-CCSD(T) n-mer reference data and described by permutationally invariant polynomials. Covalently bonded functional groups define the bodies of the MBE, allowing each ML term to be reused wherever the same chemically defined nmer occurs. Without training on whole-dipeptide energies, the assembled MB-nrg potentials predict gas-phase Ramachandran potential energy surfaces with a pooled root-mean-square deviation (RMSD) of 1.26 kcal/mol relative to DLPNO-CCSD(T), compared with 6.65 and 5.43 kcal/mol for Amber ff14SB and ff19SB force fields, respectively. Because the MB-nrg potentials are modular, the remaining deviations from the DLPNO-CCSD(T) reference can be systematically analyzed within the MBE framework and addressed by expanding the library with additional nonbonded and higher-body terms, as demonstrated for asparagine. The library thus provides an initial set of reusable n-body building blocks for peptide potentials and a blueprint for their systematic refinement and expansion toward coupled-cluster accuracy in biomolecular simulations.

item.title: Remote N‑Substituent‑Tuned Dichotomous Diradical Scission Enables Photocatalytic Divergent Rearrangement of Allylic Aminophosphines
item.description: Organophosphorus compounds are widely prevalent in pharmaceuticals, agrochemicals, and functional materials, and phosphoranyl radicals represent a versatile platform for the construction of these valuable molecules. Although the selectivity of α- and β-scission dictates the reaction outcomes of phosphoranyl radical transformations, established strategies for tuning such fragmentation are confined to monoradical systems and rely on local structural modification at the phosphorus center. Herein, we realize remote N-substituent-controlled switching between α- and βscission pathways of phosphorus–carbon triplet diradicals and apply this concept in a visible-light energy transfer photocatalytic divergent rearrangement of allylic aminophosphines to access two structurally significant organophosphorus skeletons. Computational studies reveal that the electronic properties of N-substituents govern the geometries of phosphoranyl radicals: N-alkoxy substituents favour α-scission, whereas N-sulfonyl substituents promote β-scission. This work provides new mechanistic insights into heteroatom diradical reactivity and broadens the available tools for divergent synthesis of organophosphorus compounds.

item.title: OSC700: A GW+BSE Dataset of 700 Organic Semiconductor (OSC) Crystals with an LLM-Assisted Data Extraction Agent
item.description: Key parameters for organic optoelectronic device applications derive from the excited-state properties of molecular crystals. Data scarcity (both experimental and theoretical) limits the ability to train machine learning (ML) models to predict these properties. We present the OSC700 dataset of excited-state properties of 700 crystalline organic semiconductors (OSCs) with up to 1168 atoms in the unit cell, calculated using state-of-the-art many-body perturbation theory within the GW approximation and Bethe-Salpeter equation (GW+BSE). OSC700 contains crystals of compounds comprising C,H,N,O,F,S capable of forming a variety of molecular scaffolds and crystal packing motifs. OSC700 is larger and significantly more diverse than the earlier PAH101 dataset [Scientific Data 12, 679 (2025)]. The data records contain the fundamental gap, quasiparticle band structure, static dielectric constant, first singlet exciton energy (optical gap), first triplet exciton energy, full dielectric function, and optical absorption spectra for light polarized along the three lattice vectors. Because absorption experiments on molecular crystals are rare (as opposed to solution or amorphous phases), we developed an LLM-assisted data extraction agent in order to find and retrieve available optical gap data for the materials in OSC700. The agent was able to find experimental data for 16 materials, which we used to validate the results of our calculations. The OSC700 dataset can be used to train ML models to predict the excited-state properties of crystalline organic semiconductors and find promising materials for optoelectronic device applications.

item.title: False Confidence in Generative Samplers: Exact Physical References Expose Hidden Errors and Diagnostic Blindness
item.description: Learned samplers are increasingly proposed for equilibrium sampling and free energies in chemistry, and they are usually judged by self-normalized diagnostics such as the effective sample size (ESS). We show with an elementary proposition that these diagnostics are structurally invariant to the Boltzmann mass α of unvisited basins: conditioned on not proposing a basin, the importance weights follow the law of the truncated system, so the ESS stays high while the free energy shifts by −kBT log(1 − α) and the nominal deltamethod interval contracts around the biased value, yielding asymptotically zero coverage. In a toy double well where one basin holds 49.9% of the mass, a proposal putting mass 10−6 on that basin achieves a median ESS of 98% but covers the exact logZ in 0% of 400 runs. On exactly enumerated Sherrington-Kirkpatrick instances (n = 24), nominal 95% intervals from masked diffusion and a GFlowNet cover the truth in only 8% and 47% of runs at β = 2, while classical estimators and an autoregressive network (VAN-MADE) stay near 95%. A reverse check that scores the proposal on draws from an independent reference sampler flags the dropped basin where the forward Jensen gap is blind. We demonstrate this on a continuous molecular model: a RealNVP Boltzmann generator trained on the alanine dipeptide Ramachandran landscape drops the C7ax basin (8.1% mass), reporting a median ESS of 79% with only 10% coverage, while the reverse check detects the omission (Grev = 11.7 nats). Finally, we size the bound on macromolecular systems (chignolin, Trpcage, LJ38), contrasting single-trajectory kinetic trapping with converged Anton and NMR equilibrium baselines to show that dropped macroscopic states shift free energies by 0.68 to 1.02 kcal/mol, exceeding lead-optimization thresholds.

item.title: FROST III: certified Hartree–Fock limits of diatomic molecules
item.description: We extend FROST (Fock radial orbital shooting with Taylor series) from atoms to diatomic molecules and obtain the Hartree–Fock (HF) energy of H2 at the internuclear distance R = 1.4 bohr to 103 significant figures, that of HeH+ to 101 and that of LiH to 26, each certified by an exact upper bound, where about 11, 9 and 12 figures were known before. In prolate spheroidal coordinates both nuclear cusps are absorbed and the nuclear attraction becomes linear. Expanding the orbitals and their pair potentials in Legendre polynomials of the angular coordinate η then turns the HF equations into ordinary differential equations in ξ that all have the form (ξ2−1)u′′+2ξu′ = g. This is the molecular counterpart of the radial equations of the earlier papers, with a regular singular point on the internuclear axis instead of the nucleus. The expansion of the orbitals is the only truncation besides the wall, and it is variational, while that of the potentials is exact, because Poisson’s equation is diagonal in the Legendre index. The equations are solved by the Taylor-series multiple shooting and homotopy of the atomic code, with no basis-set matrix and no self-consistentfield iteration. What is new is step control that resolves the rapidly growing Legendre modes of the high-order potentials, and a homotopy and wall continuation on a few channels only, after which a single stage on all channels, whose Jacobian is factorised in double precision, reaches the target accuracy. The certificate evaluates the energy of the piecewise-polynomial orbitals exactly: the oneelectron integrals are rational, and Neumann’s expansion of 1/r12 gives the Coulomb and exchange integrals as rationals plus rational multiples of logarithms of the knots, which are rounded outwards. The rate at which the energy converges in the number of Legendre channels is set by the complex singularities of the HF orbitals near each nucleus, found for helium in the first paper. Mapped onto the η interval, they predict the decay of the Legendre channels of H2, HeH+ and LiH to within 6%, with no adjustable parameter, and they show why LiH, and molecules of heavier atoms generally, need many more channels.

item.title: Scalable Density-Based Bootstrap Embedding with Perturbative Triples for Large Molecular Systems
item.description: Extending density-based bootstrap embedding (BE) with perturbative triples to large molecules requires control of both fragment solver cost and tensor storage. We present a restricted and unrestricted BE-CCSD(T) implementation combining density-fitted embedding transformations, fragment parallelism, and streamed contractions of triples density contributions. Explicit one-and two-particle terms and the correction to the coupled-cluster multipliers are retained without assembling a molecular two-particle density matrix or storing a complete triples tensor. Fixed-order fragmentation bounds the local correlated problem under stated locality assumptions, while blockwise evaluation controls temporary storage. Timings for

item.title: All-Dielectric Metasurfaces in Fundamentals, Materials, and Emerging Applications
item.description: The field of optics is undergoing a transformative shift, pushed forward by the demand for miniaturized, lightweight, and highly functional components. Dielectric metasurfaces have emerged as a transformative platform in modern photonics, offering unprecedented control over the amplitude, phase, polarization, and frequency of light within an ultrathin, planar architecture. Unlike their metallic predecessors, all-dielectric metasurfaces exploit Mie resonances, bound states in the continuum, and multipolar interference to achieve low-loss, high-efficiency optical functionalities across the visible, near-infrared, and terahertz spectral ranges. This review covers the field systematically, starting with the common working principles of dielectric metasurfaces and the physical mechanisms that make them so versatile. We then discuss the most widely used material platforms, including their optical properties and practical trade-offs, followed by an overview of the fabrication techniques available today. We look at both traditional top-down methods, such as electron-beam lithography, and emerging high-throughput approaches like nanoimprint lithography and photochemical deposition. We also examine the design strategies and element geometries used to build optical functionality into these surfaces, from simple phase-shifting pillars to more complex resonant architectures. Finally, this review examines the broad range of applications these structures enable, from metalenses and holography to nonlinear optics, biosensing, and terahertz generation. By identifying the key open challenges in fabrication scalability, broadband operation, and active tunability, this review aims to serve both as a reference resource for specialists and as an entry point for researchers from adjacent disciplines, charting a clear roadmap for the next decade of flat-optics research.

item.title: Applicability Domain of Universal Machine Learning Interatomic Potentials at Solid-State Battery Interfaces
item.description: Universal machine learning interatomic potentials (uMLIPs) are trained predominantly on bulk systems, yet are increasingly applied to solid-solid interfaces. Evaluating six uMLIPs against DFT across 24 Li-metal/solid-electrolyte interfaces, we map their applicability domain (AD) and where they break down. Total energies are predicted reasonably well (MAE < 15 meV/atom), whereas interatomic forces at the interfaces are not. Most models underestimate the interfacial formation energy by 0.32 J/m2 and overestimate the work of adhesion by 0.26 J/m2, and none reproduces the stability ordering of polyanion-containing interfaces. Despite large force errors for the interfaces, Li-ion kinetics agree well across models. The errors concentrate on the interface atoms and are larger for the polyanion chemistries. Descriptor-based analysis traces the higher force errors to interfacial environments that lie outside the pretraining data. Fine-tuning can close the accuracy gap, but only with data that samples the bonding across the interface, whereas slab data alone degrades performance. All models struggle on the same chemistries irrespective of the architecture, indicating the coverage of the pretraining data as the primary limitation. Overall, pretrained uMLIPs are suitable for qualitative screening of interfaces with simple single anion electrolytes, while those containing polyanions require interface-specific data.

item.title: Structure – Stability Relationships in Aryl- and Heteroarylmethanesulfonyl Chlorides and Fluorides
item.description: Sulfonyl chlorides are among the most widely used yet least storable building blocks in medicinal chemistry, and arylmethanesulfonyl chlorides in particular remain poorly represented in commercial catalogs because of their limited stability. In this work, the long-term stability of 23 aryl- and 36 heteroarylmethanesulfonyl chlorides and fluorides was evaluated systematically. Decomposition was monitored by 1H NMR spectroscopy in THF-d8 solution at 4 °C and 23 °C for up to 12 months; the solvent was chosen to avoid solvolysis and acidic admixtures, and to minimize water uptake. Whereas at least one batch of each compound remained unchanged in neat form for up to 14 years (median 5.5 years), their stability in solution varied widely, i.e., from complete decomposition of a pyridine derivative within one month to no detectable change over more than 12 months, and was governed by both the electronic nature and the position of the substituent. Notably, both strongly electron-withdrawing and strongly electron-donating substituents proved destabilizing, and the decomposition products differed accordingly: sulfonic acids for electron-poor and benzyl chlorides for electron-rich substrates. Sulfonyl fluorides proved considerably more robust: all heteroaromatic derivatives studied, except isothiazole (8% after 12 months) and pyridine (15% within one week), showed no detectable decomposition over 12 months. We believe that the resulting stability map, which assigns each compound to a defined storage class, will make arylmethanesulfonyl halides practical building blocks for early drug discovery in the near future.

item.title: The Copper(I)-catalyzed Alkyne-azide Cycloaddition “Click” Reaction in Water Requires the Formation of Two Distinct Mononuclear Copper(I) Complexes
item.description: The copper-catalyzed azide-alkyne cycloaddition (CuAAC) has seen widespread adoption amongst numerous fields, but mechanistic details remain elusive and controversial. Using a series of experiments involving fluorogenic coumarin derivatives under pseudo-first order conditions, it was determined that the reaction in conditions close to a physiological environment does not proceed according to the accepted mechanism, but rather requires azide chelation to form a mononuclear copper(I)-azide complex as a preliminary step. Stopped flow studies with a copper-chelating azide further enhanced our understanding of the reaction mechanism, emphasizing the importance of copper-alkyne chelation in which a mononuclear copper(I)-alkyne complex is formed. After both copper(I)-azide and copper(I)-alkyne complexes are formed, they come together to yield the triazole product. This mechanistic proposal of CuAAC in conditions close to a physiological environment is distinct from the currently accepted general model, which proposes dual activation of the alkyne by copper(I) followed by azide interaction. Please note that this manuscript was rejected by several leading chemistry journals for publication in 2015 due to its challenging of existing click chemistry mechanisms. The authors decided to release it to ChemRxiv as a reference for others with a purpose of assisting their experimental designs for bioconjugation.

item.title: Machine Learning for NMR Observables Sensitive to Nuclear Quantum Effects
item.description: Nuclear quantum effects (NQEs) are essential for an accurate description of systems containing light elements. Their omission in classical simulations can lead to significant deviations between theoretical predictions and experimental measurements, particularly for nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) observables that are highly sensitive to quantum nuclear motion. Although NQEs can be treated rigorously by using ab initio path-integral molecular dynamics (AI-PIMD), the substantial computational cost associated with these simulations continues to limit their applicability to large systems and long timescales. To address this limitation, we developed a machine learning-driven PIMD (MLPIMD) workflow for the accurate and efficient prediction of NMR observables, in which NQEs at finite temperature are explicitly included. As a demonstration, we investigate the experimentally measured isotropic chemical shifts, δiso, of the 3He monomer (3He@C706- ) and dimer (3He2@C706- ) endohedral fullerene hexaanions. The resulting predictions show excellent agreement with the experiment and reveal a pronounced influence of NQEs on the 3He chemical shifts in both systems. In particular, NQEs are found to play a key role in determining the chemical-shift difference between the monomer and dimer species. The methodology introduced here is broadly applicable and provides a general framework for investigating NMR observables sensitive to NQEs in complex molecular systems.

item.title: The Evolution of Electronic Structure in Conjugated Molecules Revealed by Mixed-Reference Spin-Flip Time-Dependent Density Functional Theory and Density-Based Analyses: II. Polyacenes
item.description: Large conjugated molecules feature small gaps between occupied and virtual orbital spaces, which results in complex electronic structure patterns in their low-lying states. These orbital near-degeneracies also challenge quantum chemistry methods. Mixed-reference spin-flip TDDFT (MRSF-TDDFT) and density-matrix-based analyses provide useful tools to interrogate electronic structure in large conjugated molecules. This paper investigates one such family—polyacenes. Following our recent study of the ground and low-lying excited states of all-trans polyenes, we track this evolution from benzene to dodecacene using MRSF-TDDFT and densitymatrix-based analyses. In polyacenes, the ground state acquires diradical character as the number of rings increases, while the doubly excited state dominated by the HOMO2 → LUMO2 configuration drops steeply in energy and falls below the La state between nonacene and decacene. MRSF-TDDFT reproduces the experimental La/Lb crossing, which standard linear-response TDDFT misses, and gives singlettriplet gaps close to high-level wave-function benchmarks and singlet-fission energetics consistent with experiment. The analyses show that La remains predominantly singly excited throughout the series and we attribute the strong decrease in its oscillator strength to the growing diradical character of the ground state. The doubly excited state evolves from mixed character in naphthalene, similar to the 2 1Ag− state of the polyenes, to a nearly closed-shell doubly excited state in pentacene and hexacene, and finally to a state with natural orbital occupations resembling those of the ground state in the longest acenes.
